beats.narration_text: CueGate will be a subtitle checker with a repair loop. It will find every line a viewer can't read in time, fix the timing first, shorten text only where it must, and refuse to ship any line it can't prove fits. It will exist as a Python package, a command-line tool, a small web app, and an evaluation report.

beats.narration_text: Streaming platforms publish hard, numeric rules for subtitles: how fast a line can be read, the gap between lines, how timing behaves at a cut. Break them, and delivery guides say the file gets rejected.

beats.narration_text: I checked what exists. Subtitle Edit and Editsub offer AI that shortens one line when you ask, and EZTitles runs automated QC that flags reading-speed problems. In the tools I checked, shortening is something a person triggers, one line at a time. CueGate will be a gate over the whole file, and it will publish how often its shortened lines changed meaning.

beats.narration_text: The person who'll open it is a subtitle QC lead at a localization vendor. In the first sixty seconds, they'll drop in a failing subtitle file along with the film, and they'll get back a table: every broken rule, every line fixed and how, and every line CueGate will refuse to touch, with the reason.

beats.narration_text: The order matters. First, timing: can the line stay up longer without crossing a cut or crowding the next one? Only if that fails will Claude be asked for shorter versions, with an exact character budget. Then a plain counter will check every one. The model will propose. The counter will decide.

beats.narration_text: A counter can only know a line is short enough. It can't know if it means the same thing. Look at the reply I got. It fit the budget, and it kept both negatives. But "I really don't think we should" became "Not in there": a hedged opinion turned into a flat refusal. And "what happened" became "that". That shift in tone is exactly what a character count can't see.

beats.narration_text: So CueGate will check that numbers, names and every "not" survive, then run a second, weaker meaning check. I'll measure how often that check is wrong by labelling a hundred lines myself, and I'll publish the number even if it's bad.

beats.narration_text: If it works, a reviewer could fairly conclude I can write a prompt contract with a hard budget, build a verifier the model can't argue with, run an agent loop that fails closed, tie every flag to the guideline it comes from, and evaluate it against baselines. The evidence will be the tests, the evaluation report, and the audit labels.

beats.narration_text: One thing it won't do is translate. It will work inside one language. The first piece I'll make run is the checker alone, on the English subtitles of an open Blender film. You'll know it ran because its counts will match lines I've checked by hand.

beats.narration_text: What could sink it is shot detection. Fades and fast motion can fool cut detectors, and a fake cut means the wrong timing rules. If that happens, I'll accept a cut list instead, and report detector errors separately.

beats.narration_text: It's a mix. Evaluation harnesses and prompt regression testing are skills I already have from my co-op, but that work isn't public, so I can't show it here. What I can show is the timeline gate in my Reallocation Engine recipe for this course, which I built with Claude Code. For evaluation specifically, the evidence will be this project's own test suite. What's new to me is frame-accurate timing, shot detection, subtitle standards, and checking meaning with an NLI model.
